title: Coulomb blockade-like transport and enhanced memory in organic transistors embedded with sub-nm Pt nanoparticles for neuromorphic computing
authors: Arash Ghobadi, Thomas B. Kallaos, Abhi Abhijeet, Stephen C. Klue, Joseph C. Mathai, Carsten A. Ullrich, Shubhra Gangopadhyay, Suchismita Guha
abstract: Organic transistors are playing an increasingly important role for neuromorphic applications. However, devices that rely solely on ferroelectric switching or on interface traps for their multi-conductance states exhibit limited memory windows. Here, we introduce an ultrathin oxide layer with a uniform distribution of sub-nm platinum nanoparticles (PtNPs) at the interface of a polymer semiconducting and a ferroelectric dielectric in a thin film transistor architecture. The interfacial stack, Al$_2$O$_3$/PtNP/Al$_2$O$_3$, provides a viable route for localized charge trapping and de-trapping in a region where it can most effectively influence the channel conductance. The organic transistors display a large memory window (> 20 V) in their current-voltage characteristics. The sub-nm PtNPs give rise to features that are consistent with room temperature Coulomb blockade-like transport, supporting discrete and well-separated levels within the memory window. The devices support multimodal programming using electrical and optical stimuli with both long-term plasticity and enhanced short-term plasticity (STP) phenomena. These results open new directions for implementing STP in the development of neuromorphic computing.
summary: This work engineers organic transistors by embedding sub-nanometer platinum nanoparticles (PtNPs) at the dielectric interface to enhance memory and control charge trapping. The resulting devices exhibit Coulomb blockade-like transport and a large memory window, allowing them to mimic complex biological synaptic functions like Short-Term Plasticity. This paves a new route for developing next-generation neuromorphic hardware.
main_problem: Developing organic transistors for neuromorphic computing that exhibit enhanced memory and support complex synaptic plasticity (like Short-Term Plasticity, STP).
main_result: The incorporation of sub-nm Pt nanoparticles into the dielectric interface creates a robust memory window and enables multimodal programming, mimicking biological synaptic behavior.
method: The study involves fabricating thin-film transistors using organic semiconductors and ferroelectric dielectrics, followed by electrical and optical characterization.
model_or_system: The physical system is an organic thin-film transistor utilizing an interfacial stack of Al2O3/PtNP/Al2O3 between a polymer semiconductor and a ferroelectric dielectric.
key_observables: Large memory window (> 20 V), Coulomb blockade-like transport plateaus, current spikes, and measurable synaptic weight updates via optical and electrical stimuli.
important_parameters: Sub-nm PtNP size (e.g., 0.7 nm), dielectric thickness (2 nm or 3 nm Al2O3), and operating voltages (up to 20 V).
main_assumptions: The PtNPs create a localized charge trapping/de-trapping region that effectively influences the channel conductance, enabling discrete charge states.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the device architecture, HRTEM images of PtNPs, transfer characteristics showing hysteresis, and I-V sweeps demonstrating quantized current plateaus and photo-electrical response.
paper_structure: The paper details the fabrication process, presents electrical characterization (I-V sweeps, transfer curves), analyzes the quantum-like transport features (Coulomb blockade), and finally demonstrates the application to synaptic plasticity using both electrical and optical stimuli.
why_interesting: The study bridges solid-state physics (Coulomb blockade, charge trapping) with computational neuroscience, providing an experimental platform for studying non-equilibrium charge dynamics relevant to artificial synapses.
